items.question: How did you envision your long-term research direction when you finished graduate school?
items.object: Human intelligence as inspiration for a career in AI research
items.answer: When I graduated from grad school, I really thought the rest of my entire career would be towards solving that single problem, which is: a lot of AI as a field, as a discipline, is inspired by human intelligence.

items.question: What led you and Justin Johnson to commit to founding World Labs to build world models and spatial intelligence?
items.object: The decision to found World Labs with Justin Johnson
items.answer: More than two years ago, I think both independently, both of us had been looking at the development of the large models and thinking about what's beyond language models. This idea of building world models, spatial intelligence, really was natural for us. So we started talking and decided that we should just put all the eggs in one basket and focus on solving this problem, and started World Labs together.

items.question: How do you see the role of open science in today's AI research ecosystem?
items.object: Open science in today's AI research ecosystem
items.answer: I think open science still is important. AI, obviously, compared to the image at that time, has really evolved. That was such a niche computer science discipline; now it's civilizational technology. I'll give you an example: recently my Stanford lab just announced an open dataset and benchmark called BEHAVIOR, for benchmarking robotic learning in simulated environments. That is a very clear effort in still keeping up this open science model of doing things, especially in academia. But it's important to recognize the ecosystem is a mixture. A lot of the very focused work in industry—some of them are more seeing the daylight in the form of a product than an open challenge per se.

items.question: How do you think about the health of the AI research ecosystem as commercial labs grow?
items.object: The balance between public academic AI research and commercial AI development
items.answer: I do have concerns, less about the pressure. It's more about the resourcing and the imbalanced resourcing of academia. This is a little bit of a different conversation from World Labs. I have been the past few years advocating for resourcing the healthy ecosystem. As the founding co-director of Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI, Stanford HAI, I've been working with policymakers about resourcing public sector and academic AI work. We worked with the first Trump administration on this bill called the National AI Research Resource, NAIRR, which is scoping out a national AI compute cloud as well as data repository. I also think open-source and open datasets continue to be an important part of the ecosystem. Like I said, right now in my Stanford lab, we are doing the open dataset, open benchmark on robotic learning called BEHAVIOR, and many of my colleagues are still doing that. I think that's part of the ecosystem. I think what the industry is doing, and some startups are doing, running fast with models and creating products, is also a good thing. For example, when Justin was a PhD student with me, none of the computer vision programs worked that well, right? We could write beautiful papers.

items.question: How do you see academia’s role in AI research today?
items.object: Academia’s role in AI research
items.answer: Academia has a role to play in understanding the theoretical underpinning of these large models. We still know so little about this, or extending to the interdisciplinary. Justin calls them wacky ideas. There's a lot of basic science ideas. There's a lot of blue-sky problems. So I agree. I don't think the problem is open versus closed, productization versus open sourcing. I think the problem right now is that academia by itself is severely under-resourced. The researchers and students do not have enough resources to try these ideas.

items.question: How did you approach moving beyond ImageNet object recognition toward telling the story of an image in natural language?
items.object: Moving beyond ImageNet object recognition to telling stories about images in natural language
items.answer: Andre and I were looking at what is beyond ImageNet object recognition, and at that time the convolutional neural network had proven some power in ImageNet tasks. So ConvNet is a great way to represent images. In the meantime, an early sequential model in language, called LSTM, was also being experimented with. Andre and I were talking about this long-term dream of mine. I thought it would take 100 years to solve, which is telling the story of images. When I graduated from grad school, I really thought the rest of my entire career would be towards solving that single problem: given a picture or a scene, tell the story in natural language. But things evolved so fast. When Andre started, we thought maybe combining the representation of a convolutional neural network as well as the language sequential model of LSTM, we might be able to learn through training to match captions with images. I don't remember if it was 2014 or 2015. It was CVPR 2015, the captioning paper. It was our first paper that Andre got to work: given an image, the image is represented with ConvNet, the language model is the LSTM model, and then we combine it and it's able to generate one sentence. That was one of the first times.

items.question: Why did you want to extend image captioning into dense captioning?
items.object: Dense captioning
items.answer: We wanted to extend the image-captioning work. I remember at that time we had a sense of space, because we felt captioning does not capture different parts of the image. I was talking to Justin and Andre about what we ended up calling dense captioning, which is describing the scene in greater detail, especially different parts of the scene.

items.question: How do you see spatial intelligence as different from language modeling?

items.question: How do you think about whether a generative world model needs to understand the physical structures it renders?
items.object: Physical understanding in generative world models such as Marble
items.answer: But does the model actually understand how the arch is drawing on the center kind of like stone, and the actual physical structure of it? And the other question is, does it matter that it understands it as long as it always renders something that would fit the physical model that we imagine? If you use the word understand the way you understand, I'm pretty sure the model doesn't understand it. The model is learning from the data, learning from the pattern. Does it matter, especially for the use cases? It's a good question. For now, I don't think it matters, because it renders out what you need, assuming it's perfect.

items.question: How do you see Marble fitting into your broader vision of spatial intelligence?
items.object: Marble’s role in World Labs’ vision of spatial intelligence
items.answer: So Marble is a glimpse into our model. We are a spatial intelligence model company. We believe spatial intelligence is the next frontier. In order to make spatially intelligent models, the model has to be very powerful in its ability to understand, reason, and generate in a very multimodal fashion of worlds, as well as allow the level of interactivity that we eventually hope to be as complex as how humans can interact with the world. That's the grand vision of spatial intelligence, as well as the kind of world models we see. Marble is the first glimpse into that. It's the first part of that journey. It's the first in-class model in the world that generates 3D worlds at this level of fidelity in the hands of the public. It's the starting point. We actually wrote this tech blog. Justin spent a lot of time writing that tech blog. Justin really broke it down into what are the inputs—we can have multimodal inputs of Marble—what are the kinds of editability, which allows the user to be interactive with the model, and what are the kinds of outputs we can have.

items.question: How do you see Marble helping address the shortage of training data for embodied agents?
items.object: Marble’s potential to generate simulated worlds for embodied-agent training
items.answer: Robotic training really lacks data. High-fidelity real-world data is absolutely very critical, but you're just not going to get a ton of that. The other extreme is purely internet video data; then you lack a lot of the controllability that you want to train your embodied agents with. Simulation and synthetic data is a very important middle ground for that. I've been working in this space for many years, and one of the biggest pain points is where do you get this synthetic simulated data? You have to curate assets and build and compose these complex situations. In robotics, you want a lot of different states. You want the embodied agent to interact in the synthetic environment. Marble actually has potential for helping to generate these synthetic simulated worlds for embodied agent training.

items.question: How do you understand spatial intelligence in relation to linguistic intelligence?
items.object: Spatial intelligence and its relationship to linguistic intelligence
items.answer: For me, when I think about spatial intelligence, I see it as complementary to language intelligence. I personally would not say it's spatial versus traditional because I don't know what “traditional” means. I do think spatial is complementary to linguistic. How do we define spatial intelligence? It's the capability that allows you to reason, understand, move, and interact in space. I use the example of the deduction of DNA structure. Of course, I'm simplifying this story, but a lot of that had to do with the spatial reasoning of the molecules and the chemical bonds in a 3D space to eventually conjecture a double helix, and that ability that Francis Crick and Watson had. It is very hard to reduce that process into pure language. That's a pinnacle of a civilizational moment. But every day, I'm here trying to grasp a mug. This whole process of seeing the mug, seeing the context where it is, seeing my own hand, opening my hand that geometrically would match the mug and touching the right affordance point—this is all deeply spatial. It's very hard. I'm trying to use language to narrate it. But that narrated language itself cannot get you to pick up a mug.

items.question: How do you understand spatial intelligence as a fundamental capability of AI?
items.object: Spatial intelligence
items.answer: Spatial intelligence to me is the ability to understand, reason, interact, and generate 3D worlds, because our world fundamentally, no matter how you say we can project it, fundamentally is 3D. And it's 3D because physically it's 3D, and digitally, if there is a true 3D representation, then we can make a lot of things happen more easily, whether it's designing, more creation, navigation, simulation, or the experiencing of AR, VR. All this to me is part of spatial intelligence. And again, I think what really excites me is humans have spatial intelligence. It's part of our core intelligent capabilities. Animals have spatial intelligence. The entire journey of evolution also is deeply intertwined with the evolution of spatial intelligence. So it's so fundamental. Without spatial intelligence, AI would be incomplete.

items.question: How do you think about spatial intelligence as a challenge for animals, including humans?
items.object: Spatial intelligence
items.answer:
I think from a neural and cognitive science point of view that spatial intelligence is a really hard problem that evolution has to solve for animals. And what's really interesting is I think animals have solved it to an extent, but not fully solved it. It's one of the hardest problems because what is the problem an animal has to solve? Animals have to evolve the capability of collecting light in something which we call eyes, mostly. And then with that collection of eyes, it has to reconstruct a 3D world in their mind somehow so that they can navigate and they can do things, and of course they can interact. For humans, we're the most capable animal in terms of manipulation. We can do a lot of things, and all this is spatial intelligence. To me, that's just rooted in our intelligence. What is interesting is it's not a fully solved problem even in animals. For humans, for example, if I ask you to close your eyes right now and draw out or build a 3D model of the environment around you, it's not that easy. We don't have that much capability to generate extremely complicated 3D models till we get trained.

You know, there are some of us, whether they're architects or designers or just people with a lot of training and a lot of talent, and that's a hard thing to do. And imagine you do it at your fingertip much more easily and allow much more fluid interactivity and editability. That would just be a whole different world for people, no pun intended.

items.question: How do you think about the mix of data needed to train robots?
items.object: Data for training robots, including simulation and haptics
items.answer: Some people call it data pyramids or data cakes or whatever. I agree. I think it's going to be a hybrid of many different forms of data. I also think simulation is underrated. It's actually not underrated by a lot of experts and people in the field. If you look at a lot of robotics companies, they are working on simulation and synthetic data. I also think we have to be aware that unlike language models or even unlike spatial intelligence foundation models, robotics is a highly multimodal system. What is truly underappreciated, in my opinion, is haptics. There's so much, especially if we want to do manipulation, not just navigation. I think haptics data and the ability to really integrate haptics into vision and perception and spatial data is absolutely critical.

items.question: How do you expect the physical forms of robots to evolve as robotics becomes more widespread?
items.object: The diversity of future robot form factors
items.answer: I think we're going to gradient descend into optimization of productivity and efficiency. My hypothesis is that the requirements of different tasks are so vast that having very few forms or sticking with one form is energy inefficient, and a lot of tasks can be done and should be done by much more energy-efficient form factors. Just an extreme and trivial example: if we put robots underwater, they should not be in the shape of humans. They better be in the shape of fish, right? Just think about energy efficiency. And the same with flying. Our airplanes are becoming more and more robots. And so I do think there's going to be diversity.

items.question: Why do you see creative work as an exciting commercial application of AI and spatial intelligence?
items.object: AI and spatial intelligence as collaborators in creative work
items.answer: I believe creativity is a vastly exciting area where humans can be superpowered by AI and by spatial intelligence. And here I draw an analogy with software engineering. If you look at today's success of LLMs in software engineering, including applications like Cursor and Windsurf and all that, what you see is a lot of collaboration between AI and humans, and then the collaboration comes in different levels of skill sets and all that. And I think creativity will be similar, whether we're talking about designers, 3D artists, VFX artists, or even marketing talents and game developers. There's so much need in co-designing and creating 3D space, and this is fundamentally such a hard problem even for the trained, skilled people that having a collaborator will be extremely fun if we do it right. And so I see creativity as an area that is really exciting.

items.question: What do you find challenging about turning 3D models into products people use?
items.object: Turning 3D models into products people use
items.answer: I think it's kind of ironic, right? Every one of us uses 3D every day, in so many settings. Basically, you open your eye and the whole life that you experience is 3D, even when we type on the computer or stare at a screen all the time. Yet it's still not as easy a form factor to deliver in the hands of people compared to language. items.question: How did you think about the amount of data needed to make object recognition work during your PhD?
items.object: The scale and creation of the object-recognition dataset in Fei-Fei Li's PhD research
items.answer:
Well, gosh, it goes back to 2003-ish, and the world was just barely scratching the surface of the internet, and data was not much of a thing. But doing computer vision, my PhD work was really trying to get object recognition to work. That's the problem of calling out cats and dogs and microwaves and chairs and all that when you're presented with a picture, and we were beginning to hypothesize that data matters. But we had no idea. There's no scaling law. We had no idea how far data can go.

All we wanted is, if we have a machine learning algorithm, whether it's a neural network or Bayes net, that at that time was very popular, or support vector machine, we need some data to train, and there was no data to train. And as a PhD student you want to graduate, and Petra was like, "Well, Fei, curate a dataset." And I was thinking, yeah, I do need to curate a dataset because every dataset out there is so tiny, I'm just not convinced. And Petra and I were just talking, you know, is it 15 different things or 30 different things? And then, God forbid, the PhD advisor said the three-digit number 100. And I was like, you know, that's a lot of work. But deep in my heart, I know he's right from a mathematical point of view: pushing the model to generalize, we need enough data at least.

So I did write about this process in my book, The Worlds I See, that I stumbled upon a dictionary somehow, and it really was for my own English study. The dictionary, I think it's the Webster dictionary, if I'm not wrong, just kind of randomly has depictions, visual depictions of some words. I don't even know what rule they follow, to be honest. Some are flowers, some of bicycles, some are dogs. And I was like, okay, this is actually—you can call it a cheater or a tool. I grabbed 101 of those words. And that really made my PhD advisor kind of chuckle because he's like, "Ah, yeah, you just want to do one more than I asked for, to dare me." So that's what I did. And I gotta say that I still remember I downloaded, or tried from Google—and Google was so new at that point, and the Google image search was so terrible at that point compared to today—and I had to do so much cleaning. At some point I got so desperate I just asked my mom to clean the images because I wrote a little interface on the computer. She doesn't know computers, but at least she knows click, click. So she helped me do some of that.

items.question: What makes your experience with ImageNet feel validating to you as a scientist?
items.object: The ImageNet journey and scientific validation
items.answer: Of course, ImageNet, that is one of those images that consists of multiple moments, from the early struggles and being told I will not get tenure, to actually realizing Amazon Mechanical Turk comes to rescue you, to the moment of AlexNet winning, and also to a couple of years ago, I was at an event in Toronto with Jeff Hinton and he said publicly how that was so defining, and he was almost a little bit apologetic that ImageNet was not as recognized as neural networks. So that journey is very validating, and for scientists the validation is not about recognition or awards. It's that you made a difference, that conjecture that no one believed in, that hypothesis that no one believed in, we were able to make it happen.

items.question: Why were your students Andre and Justin Johnson’s dissertations on image captioning such a significant moment for you?
items.object: Andre and Justin Johnson’s dissertations on image captioning
items.answer: Another moment I'm very proud of was actually Andre and also Justin Johnson and their dissertations. It's where, in my opinion, the first time that language and images converged by captioning and writing stories of the visual world. It was significant for me for two reasons. One is that I literally thought, I kid you not, at the end of my PhD, I thought if I can live till 100 years old, that was the problem we might be able to solve, which is storytelling of pictures. So I entered my career, like my first year assistant professor, thinking, okay, I'm going to do ImageNet to solve object recognition, and then I'm going to spend the rest of my entire career solving this problem of storytelling. And then by the time Andre and, a little later, Justin Johnson entered my lab, that was around 2013, 2014, the beginning of deep learning, and then suddenly the combination of sequential model—at that point it's LSTM, not transformer models—and CNN just blasted open the image captioning work. My work was the first, together with Google's, that was out of the door, and that really, to me, I almost had—it made me so proud. I almost had a crisis, which is like, what am I going to do for the rest of my 70 years or 65 years? So that was really exciting, how fast the field has evolved.

items.question: How do you understand the fearlessness you bring to tackling spatial intelligence at World Labs?
items.object: Fearlessness in pursuing ambitious problems
items.answer: Sometimes fearless is this very interesting position where you're somewhat delusional and crazy, but somewhat just rationally bold, and it kind of is in between, because if you're too rational, it's not courageous enough. You're not identifying problems that are big enough. But if you're completely crazy, then I don't know, there are so many things that can go wrong. So be fearless, be courageous. To me, that is, even as old as I am, how I feel I started my startup, World Labs: I want to be fearless and solve this problem of spatial intelligence.

items.question: Why do you value diversity of thinking when hiring for World Labs?
items.object: Diversity of thinking in hiring at World Labs
items.answer: First of all, we really do hire in diversity of thinking. And this is where, you know, you call us an AI company, but if you look under the hood, we've got computer graphics experts, we've got computer vision experts, we've got data experts, we've got generative AI experts, we've got machine learning infrastructure experts, we've got optimization. So it's actually really important to hire a diverse group of really talented people, because a problem as hard as spatial intelligence is not a homogeneous problem. items.question: How do you recognize fearlessness in someone you're considering hiring?

items.answer: I look for fearlessness. How do you do that? How do you identify if somebody has fearlessness in their background or in their thinking processes? It's in their background. You can sense the questions they ask, if they start asking you a lot of things about, "I don't know how to get this done." items.question: What is your most optimistic vision for human-centered AI?
items.object: Human-centered AI
items.answer:
I think I want to build a world that AI collaborates with and superpowers people. I still believe our world, our human world, needs to be human-centered, you know, where love, relationship, prosperity across all communities. These are really important. Justice and all these are really important values, and I don't think any piece of machinery, whether it's AI or airplane or biotech, should take those away. But with those critical values in mind, having AI to superpower us is really important because there's so many unsolved problems. One application area I had worked on is healthcare, for example, at Stanford, right?

If you look at healthcare, from drug discovery to cure diseases to diagnosis that can reach all people in the world, to treatment that can be accessible to all people in the world, to the whole healthcare delivery, how to make aging better, how to take care of chronic diseases, how to deal with mental health, all of this. We do not have an issue of excessive humans or anything. We're lacking help. You know, we are lacking scientific discovery. We're lacking diagnosis. We're lacking precision medicine. We're lacking safer and more effective ways of healthcare delivery and aging help and all that. And that's what I believe. I think AI is a tool to help people.
